The speaker says Charvaka counted only intensity, so the joy of helping and the pleasure of scratching an itch count alike, as Bentham said in 19th-century Britain. Later 'cultured' Charvakas, he says, admitted higher pleasures. J. S. Mill, whom the lecture does not name, is the Western voice who argued the same.
British utilitarian (1748–1832) who held that only the amount of pleasure matters, not its kind. The speaker compares this to Charvaka.
Greek hedonist (about 435–356 BCE) whom the speaker names as saying much the same as Charvaka. The speaker also cites D. H. Lawrence (the transcript says 'D.S.') as a modern echo.
Not named in the lecture; added for contrast. His 'pleasure' meant calm of mind and simple living, very unlike the feast the Charvaka caricature suggests.

Later writers divide the school into the dhurta (rogue) and the susikshita (well-schooled) types. The speaker's 'educated Charvakas' belong here (his reference to the Upanishads is a garble): they allowed higher pleasures and worldly virtue.

The best-known Charvaka maxim, recorded in the Sarvadarshanasangraha: while life lasts, live happily; when the body is ash, how can it return? 'Ghee' is clarified butter, though the speaker reads it as drink. Its point is that there is no rebirth, so the pleasure must be taken now.
Dharma (duty), artha (wealth), kama (pleasure), Moksha (liberation). The speaker says Charvaka keeps only kama (some records keep artha as its means). Eight of the nine schools put Moksha highest.
Charvaka's answer to Moksha: apavarga, the end of the cycle, is simply death, with nothing after. Heaven is pleasure and hell is pain, here and now.
The speaker's praise: the only Indian school that asks whether making this life good could be enough. He calls it 'secular' in the sense of 'of this world', not in the sense of church and state.

Sarvadarshanasangraha reports Charvaka verses mocking ritual: the Vedas were made by buffoons, knaves and demons; if shraddha offerings feed the dead, feed travellers at home; if sacrificed animals go to heaven, sacrifice your parents. The speaker calls religion a 'mental illness' in their words and sets Kabir beside it. The Buddha's stand on sacrifice was milder.
All knowledge comes from experience. The speaker names Locke, Berkeley and Hume as Western supporters. Berkeley held that matter does not exist, the opposite of Charvaka's materialism.
18th-century Irish empiricist and idealist: to be is to be perceived, so there is no matter outside mind. The speaker lists him among empiricists.
Direct knowledge through the five senses, plus the mind for pleasure and pain. Charvaka's only valid source.
Seeing a wet road and concluding it rained. Charvaka said inference cannot be trusted.
Knowledge from a trusted person, as in trusting a doctor's diagnosis. Charvaka rejected it, which meant rejecting the Vedas as proof.
Learning about an unseen thing from a description and its likeness to a known one, as in recognising an elephant.
Knowledge by implication: a man fat in daylight who never eats by day must eat by night.
Knowing that something is absent, as in seeing that a person is not in the room.

Charvaka one; Buddhists and Vaisheshika two; Samkhya and Yoga three; Nyaya four; Prabhakara Mimamsa five; Bhatta Mimamsa and Advaita Vedanta six. The lecture lumps Vedanta with the three-source schools; that fits Vishishtadvaita but not Advaita.

The basis of inference: smoke always goes with fire. Charvaka asked how anyone can see every case, so no universal link is ever established; Nyaya replied with inference by long experience and by testing counter-cases.

Classic reply by Nyaya, Buddhists and Jains: to argue with an opponent, you must infer his mind from his words, so denying inference uses it. The speaker's own critique is different: perception alone cannot run a life (you would not take an umbrella or leave a burning house).

Jaundice turns white to yellow, double vision doubles, a moving train makes the platform move, the earth looks flat and the sun looks to rise. Some sounds, such as a dog whistle, are out of our range. The speaker uses all this to show senses are limited, and Charvaka's claim is overreaching.

Thoughts, emotions and atoms cannot be seen, and no one has seen the galaxies or a nuclear weapon at first hand. The speaker's reply: God or soul may be unproven, but unseen is not the same as non-existent.

The fifth element. Space cannot be touched, seen or smelt; you see objects in space, not space. So Charvaka dropped it, as the speaker says Ajita (whom he runs together with Pakudha) and Empedocles also kept four.

Greek philosopher (5th c. BCE) who taught four 'roots': earth, air, fire, water, mixed and parted by Love and Strife. The speaker pairs him with Pakudha Kaccayana, though the Pali texts give Pakudha seven elements and Ajita four.
Greek atomist (5th c. BCE) who taught that all things are atoms moving in void, with no purpose or mind behind them.
Early Greek thinker (6th c. BCE) who made air the first principle.
Greek thinker (about 500 BCE) who taught that what is cannot change or perish.
The speaker lists Thales (water), Anaximenes (air), Heraclitus (fire) and Parmenides (being) as many Western matter-thinkers; India, he says, has one clear school of materialists.
The world as a self-running process with no designer or purpose; the speaker contrasts it with creationism, which holds God made it for a purpose.

From the Sarvadarshanasangraha: grain and yeast are not intoxicating, but fermented they are; leaf, nut and lime are not red, but chewed they colour the lips. So consciousness appears when elements combine. The speaker says that using analogies is weak philosophy, though sometimes needed; critics note fermentation needs a further cause, and an analogy proves nothing.

A claim that the soul weighs 21 grams. The speaker rejects it, noting that a thought does not weigh more because you read a book. It traces to Duncan MacDougall's 1907 experiment on six dying patients, which was never reproduced.

Not named in the lecture. David Chalmers' phrase (1995) for why physical processes should come with felt experience; the speaker's own form of it is that 'iron cannot make mind', as cotton cannot make ice.
Indian communist-turned-radical-humanist (1887–1954). The speaker names him, with Marx in the West, among modern materialists.

Chemistry now lists 118 elements, of which about 90-odd occur in nature and the rest are made in labs. The speaker's point: ancient lists were hypotheses, philosophy first put the question, and nothing in knowledge is wasted.

Greek sophist (5th c. BCE) who argued nothing exists, or if it does it cannot be known or told. The speaker (name garbled in the transcript) compares this with Sanjaya's scepticism, about a century earlier.

Medieval writers often speak of three Vedas (trayi), treating the Atharvaveda as partly repeating the rest. The speaker says that when Charvaka attacks 'the three Vedas' it is not rejecting only three.

The speaker's contrast: the Vedas look outward, with many gods, prayers for cattle and long life, heaven and ritual; the Upanishads look inward, with karma, rebirth and Moksha, and send people into the forest. Other world religions also began with many gods tied to sun, fire and water.

The speaker says the best people of society leave it, and quotes this as a remark made by Vivekananda in America (I cannot confirm the source). He sees it as a reason for the restlessness of the 6th century that fed the Shramana movement.

The speaker's reply to a question: the sociology of religion explains its social use, such as meeting people, shared meals and company for the elderly and for women who rarely go out. It does not answer intellectual questions; philosophy of religion does.
Not named in the lecture; the transcript has garbled names at this point and probably means Durkheim and Weber. French founder of sociology, who read religion as the way a society holds together.
German sociologist; see the note on Durkheim. The lecture names Marx outright and two garbled names.

nodes.l: Why we do not act on what we know
nodes.d: Asked why knowledge of the right thing does not become action, the speaker answers: conscience and desire pull against each other and desire often wins; being moral takes effort, being weak does not; religion supports habit, while a thinking person must weigh every case. The Greeks called the gap akrasia.

Jains and Buddhists meditate, Vedic people perform yajna for heaven, but Charvaka, wanting nothing beyond this life, had no method of spiritual practice. The speaker separates it from Vajrayana, which seems alike in boldness but is a disciplined Buddhist path.

The speaker accepts Osho's view that the school's books were destroyed, and mentions Khilji's burning of Nalanda in the same breath. Historians have no evidence of a campaign against Charvaka books; neglect, lack of institutions and scribal choice may explain the loss as well.

The speaker: it had no monastery, no practice and no appeal of renunciation, so it could not become an institution. Buddhism fled abroad (Japan, Korea, China, Sri Lanka) and Jainism survives with about 40 lakh believers in India. Today, he says, most people live like Charvakas without the name.

nodes.l: Doubt as the root of science
nodes.d: Osho's claim, as the speaker retells it, that India would have had more scientists if Charvaka had survived. The speaker agrees history turns on accidents and that doubt is part of science's ethos; he does not claim to know what would have followed.

The speaker's roadmap for the Gita's ethics: Nishkama Karma Yoga, Sthitaprajna (the steady-minded), Lokasangraha (holding the world together) and avatarism. He advises exam candidates to name all four. This transcript develops only the first, plus Swadharma, and stops before the other three, so those nodes carry no lecture detail.

Named in the roadmap but not covered in the transcript. In the Gita (chapter 2, about verses 54–72) the term describes a person whose mind stays level in pleasure and pain; the detail here is from standard sources, not the lecture.

Named in the roadmap but not covered in the transcript. In the Gita (3.20 and 3.25) it means acting for the good of the world so that society holds together; the detail is from standard sources, not the lecture.

The speaker promises to explain its ethical side at the end, but the transcript stops before it. In the Gita (4.7–8) Krishna says he takes birth whenever right declines; the verse reference is from standard sources, not the lecture.

The Gita's best-known teaching, as the speaker puts it: act fully, but do not cling to the result. He glosses 'nishkama' as free of desire or attachment, and stresses that the detachment is from the fruit, not from the work.

Added for context. The Gita's own phrases are anasakta karma (action without attachment) and phalatyaga (giving up the fruit); 'nishkama karma' is the standard later label. Gandhi called the teaching anasaktiyoga, and Tilak's reading is titled Karmayoga.

nodes.l: Gita 2.47: the right is to the action only
nodes.d: The speaker's central verse. Its four parts as he gives them: you have a right to action alone; never to its fruits; do not make the fruit your motive; and do not cling to inaction. 'You have only the right to do your duty, not to desire the fruit.'

nodes.l: Attach to the work, detach from the result
nodes.d: The speaker's reading: 'attachment' is clinging to the outcome, and the Gita asks you to put your whole self into the act while not being driven by what it will bring. He compares it to a popular Hindi film song on doing your work and leaving the reward.

nodes.l: Detachment is a matter of degree
nodes.d: The speaker answers the charge that the teaching is impractical. Thinking in all-or-nothing terms makes total detachment impossible, and he calls that one of the most basic fallacies in logic. People stand at points on a scale: a hungry baby cries only to get fed, while a student may study for pure interest. The closer you are to the detached end, he says, the steadier your life.

nodes.l: Enjoy the process, not the result
nodes.d: The speaker's example: some students read for love of the subject and are content whatever the exam brings, while those who want only the result are anxious. His advice for an interview is to treat it as a half hour with five senior people, a chance worth enjoying. He says real happiness belongs to those who enjoy the process.

The speaker uses the term to say that if you keep thinking about being happy you will not be, as with someone who cannot sleep because of thinking about sleep. Added for context: the phrase was made current by Henry Sidgwick (The Methods of Ethics, 1874); Mill noted something similar in his Autobiography.

nodes.l: The fruit is assured by the moral order
nodes.d: The speaker says detachment does not mean there is no fruit: there is a moral system in which you get what you deserve, if not now then in a later life, so you need not worry about it. Added for context: elsewhere the Gita also asks that actions be offered to Krishna (9.27).

What the Gita means by duty, the speaker says: not a general rule of morality but the duty fitted to one's own role and nature. A soldier should fight, a king should rule, and neither should compromise the duty given to him. He says this is the message in practice: live by your Swadharma and do not think about the fruit.

The speaker's most famous line on duty (Gita 3.35, repeated in 18.47): it is better to die in one's own duty than to follow another's, which brings fear. The standard text adds that one's own duty is better even when done imperfectly; the transcript omits that clause.

The Gita ties Swadharma to svabhava, one's basic nature (chapter 18). The speaker finds this comfortable in the case of the soldier or king, and says the problem begins only when the text says duty follows the Varna.

nodes.l: The Varna problem in the Gita
nodes.d: The speaker calls this the only real difficulty in its ethics. Some sociologists, he says, hold that every society needs a religious text to support its social order, and that the Gita did so for Varna; Ambedkar is its main critic on this. The speaker calls the text a grey area: it does not say Varna goes by birth.

nodes.l: Gita 4.13: four varnas by quality and action
nodes.d: Krishna says he made the four varnas by the distribution of guna and karma (quality and action). The speaker reads this as an aptitude-based scheme. The next lines of the verse, not quoted in the lecture, call Krishna the maker yet 'not the doer'.

The speaker's thought experiment: a Varna system could be open, letting a merchant's son who tests as a scholar become a Brahmin, and a person change role in their own life. He says that if the Gita's Varna was open it is defensible, and if birth-bound it should not be supported, and admits he is no historian. Historians note that most classical commentators read the verses as birth-based, while reformers such as Dayananda argued for merit.

The speaker argues that Krishna, raised in a family of cowherds, chose to be a strategist and charioteer, which would show that roles were open. Historians point out that the Mahabharata calls Krishna a Kshatriya of the Yadava line raised among cowherds, so the example proves less than the speaker suggests.

The speaker says Ambedkar wrote generally against the Gita. Added for context: in 'Krishna and His Gita' he argued that it defended the caste order and Brahmanical reaction against Buddhism; other scholars contest this reading.

nodes.l: Judging a system by its own time
nodes.d: The speaker's caution: every age has its limits, so condemning the past by today's standards is poor history. In 500 years people will judge us as harshly. The test he proposes is whether the system allowed movement, and he adds that he would write on the subject in an exam only if asked.

Added for context. The Gita opens with Arjuna, facing kin on the other side, refusing to fight. Krishna's reply that duty must be done without clinging to the result is what the lecture's ethics rests on.
Added for context. Nationalist leader (1856–1920) whose commentary Gita Rahasya, written in jail in Mandalay and published in 1915, read the Gita as a call to action rather than withdrawal.

Added for context. Kant held that an act is right when done from duty, whatever the outcome. The Gita's Swadharma differs: it fits duty to a person's role and nature, where Kant's duty applies to all alike.

nodes.text: Karma Yoga karmayoga Path of Selfless Service The third chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Karma Yoga" or the "Path of Selfless Service". Here Lord Krishna emphasizes the importance of karma in life. He reveals that it is important for every human being to engage in some sort of activity in this material world. Further, he describes the kinds of actions that lead to bondage and the kinds that lead to liberation. Those persons who continue to perform their respective duties externally for the pleasure of the Supreme, without attachment to its rewards get liberation at the end.

nodes.text: Karma Sanyasa Yoga karmasaṃnyāsayoga Path of Renunciation The fifth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Karma Sanyasa Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna compares the paths of renunciation in actions (Karma Sanyas) and actions with detachment (Karma Yoga) and explains that both are means to reach the same goal and we can choose either. A wise person should perform his/her worldly duties without attachment to the fruits of his/her actions and dedicate them to God. This way they remain unaffected by sin and eventually attain liberation.

nodes.text: Dhyana Yoga dhyānayoga Path of Meditation The sixth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Dhyana Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna reveals the "Yoga of Meditation" and how to practise this Yoga. He discusses the role of action in preparing for Meditation, how performing duties in devotion purifies one's mind and heightens one's spiritual consciousness. He explains in detail the obstacles that one faces when trying to control their mind and the exact methods by which one can conquer their mind. He reveals how one can focus their mind on Paramatma and unite with the God.

nodes.d: The seventh chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Gyaan Vigyana Yoga ". In this chapter, Krishna reveals that he is the Supreme Truth, the principal cause and the sustaining force of everything. He reveals his illusionary energy in this material world called Maya,…
nodes.text: Gyaan Vigyana Yoga jñānavijñānayoga Self-Knowledge and Enlightenment The seventh chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Gyaan Vigyana Yoga ". In this chapter, Krishna reveals that he is the Supreme Truth, the principal cause and the sustaining force of everything. He reveals his illusionary energy in this material world called Maya, which is very difficult to overcome but those who surrender their minds unto Him attain Him easily. He also describes the four types of people who surrender to Him in devotion and the four kinds that don't. Krishna confirms that He is the Ultimate Reality and those who realize this Truth reach the pinnacle of spiritual realization and un…

nodes.d: The eighth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Akshara Brahma Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna reveals the importance of the last thought before death. If we can remember Krishna at the time of death, we will certainly attain him. Thus, it is very important to be…
nodes.sub: Path of the Eternal God · 28 verses
nodes.text: Akshara Brahma Yoga akṣarabrahmayoga Path of the Eternal God The eighth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Akshara Brahma Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna reveals the importance of the last thought before death. If we can remember Krishna at the time of death, we will certainly attain him. Thus, it is very important to be in constant awareness of the Lord at all times, thinking of Him and chanting His names at all times. By perfectly absorbing their mind in Him through constant devotion, one can go beyond this material existence to Lord's Supreme abode.

nodes.d: The ninth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Raja Vidya Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna explains that He is Supreme and how this material existence is created, maintained and destroyed by His Yogmaya and all beings come and go under his supervision. He reveals…
nodes.sub: Yoga through the King of Sciences · 34 verses
nodes.text: Raja Vidya Yoga rājavidyārājaguhyayoga Yoga through the King of Sciences The ninth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Raja Vidya Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna explains that He is Supreme and how this material existence is created, maintained and destroyed by His Yogmaya and all beings come and go under his supervision. He reveals the Role and the Importance of Bhakti (transcendental devotional service) towards our Spiritual Awakening. In such devotion, one must live for the God, offer everything that he possesses to Him and do everything for Him only. One who follows such devotion becomes free from the bonds of this material world and unites with the Lord.

nodes.d: The tenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Vibhooti Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna reveals Himself as the cause of all causes. He describes His various manifestations and opulences in order to increase Arjuna's Bhakti. Arjuna is fully convinced of Lord's par…
nodes.sub: Yoga through Appreciating the Infinite Opulences of God · 42 verses
nodes.text: Vibhooti Yoga vibhūtiyoga Yoga through Appreciating the Infinite Opulences of God The tenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Vibhooti Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna reveals Himself as the cause of all causes. He describes His various manifestations and opulences in order to increase Arjuna's Bhakti. Arjuna is fully convinced of Lord's paramount position and proclaims him to be the Supreme Personality. He prays to Krishna to describe more of His divine glories which are like nectar to hear.

nodes.d: The eleventh chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Vishwaroopa Darshana Yoga". In this chapter, Arjuna requests Krishna to reveal His Universal Cosmic Form that encompasses all the universes, the entire existence. Arjuna is granted divine vision to be able to see…
nodes.sub: Yoga through Beholding the Cosmic Form of God · 55 verses
nodes.text: Vishwaroopa Darshana Yoga viśvarūpadarśanayoga Yoga through Beholding the Cosmic Form of God The eleventh chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Vishwaroopa Darshana Yoga". In this chapter, Arjuna requests Krishna to reveal His Universal Cosmic Form that encompasses all the universes, the entire existence. Arjuna is granted divine vision to be able to see the entirety of creation in the body of the Supreme Lord Krishna.

nodes.d: The twelfth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Bhakti Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna emphasizes the superiority of Bhakti Yoga (the path of devotion) over all other types of spiritual disciplines and reveals various aspects of devotion. He further explains tha…
nodes.text: Bhakti Yoga bhaktiyoga The Yoga of Devotion The twelfth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Bhakti Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna emphasizes the superiority of Bhakti Yoga (the path of devotion) over all other types of spiritual disciplines and reveals various aspects of devotion. He further explains that the devotees who perform pure devotional service to Him, with their consciousness, merged in Him and all their actions dedicated to Him, are quickly liberated from the cycle of life and death. He also describes the various qualities of the devotees who are very dear to Him.

nodes.d: The thirteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Ksetra Ksetrajna Vibhaaga Yoga". The word "kshetra" means "the field", and the "kshetrajna" means "the knower of the field". We can think of our material body as the field and our immortal soul as the knower of…
nodes.sub: Yoga through Distinguishing the Field and the Knower of the Field · 35 verses
nodes.text: Ksetra Ksetrajna Vibhaaga Yoga kṣetra-kṣetrajñavibhāgayoga Yoga through Distinguishing the Field and the Knower of the Field The thirteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Ksetra Ksetrajna Vibhaaga Yoga". The word "kshetra" means "the field", and the "kshetrajna" means "the knower of the field". We can think of our material body as the field and our immortal soul as the knower of the field. In this chapter, Krishna discriminates between the physical body and the immortal soul. He explains that the physical body is temporary and perishable whereas the soul is permanent and eternal. The physical body can be destroyed but the soul can never be destroyed. The chapter then describes God, who is the Supreme Soul. All th…

nodes.d: The fourteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Gunatraya Vibhaga Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna reveals the three gunas (modes) of the material nature - goodness, passion and ignorance which everything in the material existence is influenced by. He further…
nodes.sub: Yoga through Understanding the Three Modes of Material Nature · 27 verses
nodes.text: Gunatraya Vibhaga Yoga guṇatrayavibhāgayoga Yoga through Understanding the Three Modes of Material Nature The fourteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Gunatraya Vibhaga Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna reveals the three gunas (modes) of the material nature - goodness, passion and ignorance which everything in the material existence is influenced by. He further explains the essential characteristics of each of these modes, their cause and how they influence a living entity affected by them. He then reveals the various characteristics of the persons who have gone beyond these gunas. The chapter ends with Krishna reminding us of the power of pure devotion to God and how attachment to God can help…

nodes.d: The fifteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Purushottama Yoga". In Sanskrit, Purusha means the "All-pervading God", and Purushottam means the timeless & transcendental aspect of God. Krishna reveals that the purpose of this Transcendental knowledge of the…
nodes.sub: The Yoga of the Supreme Divine Personality · 20 verses
nodes.text: Purushottama Yoga puruṣottamayoga The Yoga of the Supreme Divine Personality The fifteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Purushottama Yoga". In Sanskrit, Purusha means the "All-pervading God", and Purushottam means the timeless & transcendental aspect of God. Krishna reveals that the purpose of this Transcendental knowledge of the God is to detach ourselves from the bondage of the material world and to understand Krishna as the Supreme Divine Personality, who is the eternal controller and sustainer of the world. One who understands this Ultimate Truth surrenders to Him and engages in His devotional service.

nodes.d: The sixteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Daivasura Sampad Vibhaga Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna describes explicitly the two kinds of natures among human beings - divine and demoniac. Those who possess demonaic qualities associate themselves with the…
nodes.sub: Yoga through Discerning the Divine and Demoniac Natures · 24 verses
nodes.text: Daivasura Sampad Vibhaga Yoga daivāsurasampadvibhāgayoga Yoga through Discerning the Divine and Demoniac Natures The sixteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Daivasura Sampad Vibhaga Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna describes explicitly the two kinds of natures among human beings - divine and demoniac. Those who possess demonaic qualities associate themselves with the modes of passion and ignorance do not follow the regulations of the scriptures and embrace materialistic views. These people attain lower births and further material bondage. But people who possess divine qualities, follow the instructions of the scriptures, associate themselves with the mode of goodness and purify the mind through spirit…

nodes.d: The seventeenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Sraddhatraya Vibhaga Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna describes the three types of faith corresponding to the three modes of the material nature. Lord Krishna further reveals that it is the nature of faith that…
nodes.sub: Yoga through Discerning the Three Divisions of Faith · 28 verses
nodes.text: Sraddhatraya Vibhaga Yoga śraddhātrayavibhāgayoga Yoga through Discerning the Three Divisions of Faith The seventeenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Sraddhatraya Vibhaga Yoga". In this chapter, Krishna describes the three types of faith corresponding to the three modes of the material nature. Lord Krishna further reveals that it is the nature of faith that determines the quality of life and the character of living entities. Those who have faith in passion and ignorance perform actions that yield temporary, material results while those who have faith in goodness perform actions in accordance with scriptural instructions and hence their hearts get further purified.

nodes.d: The eighteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Moksha Sanyas Yoga". Arjuna requests the Lord to explain the difference between the two types of renunciations - sanyaas(renunciation of actions) and tyaag(renunciation of desires). Krishna explains that a sanya…
nodes.sub: Yoga through the Perfection of Renunciation and Surrender · 78 verses
nodes.text: Moksha Sanyaas Yoga mokṣasaṃnyāsayoga Yoga through the Perfection of Renunciation and Surrender The eighteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is "Moksha Sanyas Yoga". Arjuna requests the Lord to explain the difference between the two types of renunciations - sanyaas(renunciation of actions) and tyaag(renunciation of desires). Krishna explains that a sanyaasi is one who abandons family and society in order to practise spiritual discipline whereas a tyaagi is one who performs their duties without attachment to the rewards of their actions and dedicating them to the God. Krishna recommends the second kind of renunciation - tyaag. Krishna then gives a detailed analysis of the effects of the t…

nodes.text: The Divine Teacher, charioteer of Arjuna Speaker of the Gita — 'Śrī Bhagavān' — revealed as the Supreme Person (15.18) and as the cosmic form (Ch. 11).

nodes.text: The Blind King The blind Kuru king whose single question — 'what did my sons and the sons of Pandu do?' (1.1) — opens the Gita.

nodes.text: Kaurava crown prince Eldest son of Dhritarashtra. Surveying the armies, he addresses Drona with anxious bravado (1.3–11).

nodes.text: First recipient of the yoga 'I taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvān; Vivasvān told it to Manu; Manu to Ikṣvāku' (4.1) — the lineage of the teaching.

nodes.d: Dhritarashtra said, "What did my people and the sons of Pandu do when they had assembled together, eager for battle, on the holy plain of Kurukshetra, O Sanjaya?"
nodes.text: Dhritarashtra said, "What did my people and the sons of Pandu do when they had assembled together, eager for battle, on the holy plain of Kurukshetra, O Sanjaya?" dharmakṣetre kurukṣetre samavetā yuyutsavaḥ | māmakāḥ pāṇḍavāścaiva kimakurvata sañjaya ||

nodes.d: Sanjaya said: Having seen the army of the Pandavas drawn up in battle array, King Duryodhana approached his teacher, Drona, and spoke these words.
nodes.text: Sanjaya said: Having seen the army of the Pandavas drawn up in battle array, King Duryodhana approached his teacher, Drona, and spoke these words. dṛṣṭvā tu pāṇḍavānīkaṃ vyūḍhaṃ duryodhanastadā | ācāryamupasaṅgamya rājā vacanamabravīt ||

nodes.d: Behold, O Teacher! This mighty army of the sons of Pandu, arrayed by the son of Drupada, thy wise disciple.
nodes.text: Behold, O Teacher! This mighty army of the sons of Pandu, arrayed by the son of Drupada, thy wise disciple. paśyaitāṃ pāṇḍuputrāṇāmācārya mahatīṃ camūm | vyūḍhāṃ drupadaputreṇa tava śiṣyeṇa dhīmatā ||

nodes.d: Here are heroes, mighty archers, equal in battle to Bhima and Arjuna, Yuyudhana (Satyaki), Virata, and Drupada—all mighty warriors.
nodes.text: Here are heroes, mighty archers, equal in battle to Bhima and Arjuna, Yuyudhana (Satyaki), Virata, and Drupada—all mighty warriors. atra śūrā maheṣvāsā bhīmārjunasamā yudhi | yuyudhāno virāṭaśca drupadaśca mahārathaḥ ||

nodes.d: Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, the valiant king of Kasi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Saibya—the best of men.
nodes.text: Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, the valiant king of Kasi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Saibya—the best of men. dhṛṣṭaketuścekitānaḥ kāśirājaśca vīryavān | purujitkuntibhojaśca śaibyaśca narapuṅgavaḥ ||

nodes.d: The strong Yudhamanyu and the brave Uttamaujas, the son of Subhadra (Abhimanyu, the son of Subhadra and Arjuna), and the sons of Draupadi, all of them great charioteers (great…

nodes.d: Know also, O best among the twice-born! the names of those who are the most distinguished amongst ourselves, the leaders of my army; these I name to you for your information.
nodes.text: Know also, O best among the twice-born! the names of those who are the most distinguished amongst ourselves, the leaders of my army; these I name to you for your information. asmākaṃ tu viśiṣṭā ye tānnibodha dvijottama | nāyakā mama sainyasya saṃjñārthaṃ tānbravīmi te ||

nodes.d: "Thou thyself, Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, the victorious in war, Asvatthama, Vikarna, and Bhurisrava, the son of Somadatta—all these are ready for battle."
nodes.text: "Thou thyself, Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, the victorious in war, Asvatthama, Vikarna, and Bhurisrava, the son of Somadatta—all these are ready for battle." bhavānbhīṣmaśca karṇaśca kṛpaśca samitiñjayaḥ | aśvatthāmā vikarṇaśca saumadattistathaiva ca ||

nodes.d: And also many other heroes, ready to give up their lives for my sake, armed with various weapons and missiles, all well-skilled in battle.
nodes.text: And also many other heroes, ready to give up their lives for my sake, armed with various weapons and missiles, all well-skilled in battle. anye ca bahavaḥ śūrā madarthe tyaktajīvitāḥ | nānāśastrapraharaṇāḥ sarve yuddhaviśāradāḥ ||

nodes.d: Our army, marshalled by Bhishma, is insufficient, whereas theirs, marshalled by Bhima, is sufficient.
nodes.text: Our army, marshalled by Bhishma, is insufficient, whereas theirs, marshalled by Bhima, is sufficient. aparyāptaṃ tadasmākaṃ balaṃ bhīṣmābhirakṣitam | paryāptaṃ tvidameteṣāṃ balaṃ bhīmābhirakṣitam ||

nodes.d: Therefore, do all of you, stationed in your respective positions in the several divisions of the army, protect Bhishma alone.
nodes.text: Therefore, do all of you, stationed in your respective positions in the several divisions of the army, protect Bhishma alone. ayaneṣu ca sarveṣu yathābhāgamavasthitāḥ | bhīṣmamevābhirakṣantu bhavantaḥ sarva eva hi ||

nodes.d: His glorious grandsire, the oldest of the Kauravas, roared like a lion to cheer Duryodhana and blew his conch.
nodes.text: His glorious grandsire, the oldest of the Kauravas, roared like a lion to cheer Duryodhana and blew his conch. tasya saṃjanayanharṣaṃ kuruvṛddhaḥ pitāmahaḥ | siṃhanādaṃ vinadyoccaiḥ śaṅkhaṃ dadhmau pratāpavān ||

nodes.d: Then, suddenly, conches, kettledrums, tabors, drums, and cow horns blared forth from the Kaurava side, and the sound was tremendous.
nodes.text: Then, suddenly, conches, kettledrums, tabors, drums, and cow horns blared forth from the Kaurava side, and the sound was tremendous. tataḥ śaṅkhāśca bheryaśca paṇavānakagomukhāḥ | sahasaivābhyahanyanta sa śabdastumulo’bhavat ||

nodes.d: Then, Madhava (Krishna) and the son of Pandu (Arjuna), seated in the magnificent chariot yoked with white horses, blew divine conches.
nodes.text: Then, Madhava (Krishna) and the son of Pandu (Arjuna), seated in the magnificent chariot yoked with white horses, blew divine conches. tataḥ śvetairhayairyukte mahati syandane sthitau | mādhavaḥ pāṇḍavaścaiva divyau śaṅkhau pradadhmatuḥ ||

nodes.d: Hrishikesha blew the Panchajanya, Arjuna blew the Devadatta, and Bhima, the wolf-bellied doer of terrible deeds, blew the great conch Paundra.
nodes.text: Hrishikesha blew the Panchajanya, Arjuna blew the Devadatta, and Bhima, the wolf-bellied doer of terrible deeds, blew the great conch Paundra. pāñcajanyaṃ hṛṣīkeśo devadattaṃ dhanaṃjayaḥ | pauṇḍraṃ dadhmau mahāśaṅkhaṃ bhīmakarmā vṛkodaraḥ ||

nodes.d: King Yudhishthira, the son of Kunti, blew the Anantavijaya; Nakula and Sahadeva blew the Sughosha and the Manipushpaka.
nodes.text: King Yudhishthira, the son of Kunti, blew the Anantavijaya; Nakula and Sahadeva blew the Sughosha and the Manipushpaka. anantavijayaṃ rājā kuntīputro yudhiṣṭhiraḥ | nakulaḥ sahadevaśca sughoṣamaṇipuṣpakau ||

nodes.d: The king of Kasi, an excellent archer, Sikhandi, the mighty car-warrior, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, and Satyaki, the unconquered.
nodes.text: The king of Kasi, an excellent archer, Sikhandi, the mighty car-warrior, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, and Satyaki, the unconquered. kāśyaśca parameṣvāsaḥ śikhaṇḍī ca mahārathaḥ | dhṛṣṭadyumno virāṭaśca sātyakiścāparājitaḥ ||

nodes.d: Drupada and the sons of Draupadi, O Lord of the Earth, and the son of Subhadra, the mighty-armed, blew their conches each separately.
nodes.text: Drupada and the sons of Draupadi, O Lord of the Earth, and the son of Subhadra, the mighty-armed, blew their conches each separately. drupado draupadeyāśca sarvaśaḥ pṛthivīpate | saubhadraśca mahābāhuḥ śaṅkhāndadhmuḥ pṛthakpṛthak ||

nodes.d: The tumultuous sound rent the hearts of Dhritarashtra's party, reverberating through both heaven and earth.
nodes.text: The tumultuous sound rent the hearts of Dhritarashtra's party, reverberating through both heaven and earth. sa ghoṣo dhārtarāṣṭrāṇāṃ hṛdayāni vyadārayat | nabhaśca pṛthivīṃ caiva tumulo vyanunādayan ||

nodes.d: For I desire to observe those who are assembled here to fight, wishing to please in battle the evil-minded Duryodhana—the son of Dhritarashtra.
nodes.text: For I desire to observe those who are assembled here to fight, wishing to please in battle the evil-minded Duryodhana—the son of Dhritarashtra. yotsyamānānavekṣe’haṃ ya ete’tra samāgatāḥ | dhārtarāṣṭrasya durbuddheryuddhe priyacikīrṣavaḥ ||

nodes.d: Sanjaya said, Thus addressed by Arjuna, Krishna stationed the best of chariots, O Dhritarashtra, in the midst of the two armies.
nodes.text: Sanjaya said, Thus addressed by Arjuna, Krishna stationed the best of chariots, O Dhritarashtra, in the midst of the two armies. evamukto hṛṣīkeśo guḍākeśena bhārata | senayorubhayormadhye sthāpayitvā rathottamam ||

nodes.d: In front of Bhishma and Drona, and all the rulers of the earth, he said: "O Arjuna, son of Pritha, behold these Kurus gathered together."
nodes.text: In front of Bhishma and Drona, and all the rulers of the earth, he said: "O Arjuna, son of Pritha, behold these Kurus gathered together." bhīṣmadroṇapramukhataḥ sarveṣāṃ ca mahīkṣitām | uvāca pārtha paśyaitānsamavetānkurūniti ||

nodes.d: Then, Arjuna (son of Pritha) saw there (in the armies) stationed fathers, grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and friends.
nodes.text: Then, Arjuna (son of Pritha) saw there (in the armies) stationed fathers, grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and friends. tatrāpaśyatsthitānpārthaḥ pitṛnatha pitāmahān | ācāryānmātulānbhrātṛnputrānpautrānsakhīṃstathā ||

nodes.d: He saw fathers-in-law and friends in both the armies. The son of Kunti, Arjuna, seeing all those kinsmen thus standing arrayed, spoke sorrowfully, deeply filled with pity.
nodes.text: He saw fathers-in-law and friends in both the armies. The son of Kunti, Arjuna, seeing all those kinsmen thus standing arrayed, spoke sorrowfully, deeply filled with pity. śvaśurānsuhṛdaścaiva senayorubhayorapi | tānsamīkṣya sa kaunteyaḥ sarvānbandhūnavasthitān ||

nodes.d: Arjuna said, "O Krishna, seeing my kinsmen arrayed here, eager to fight,
nodes.text: Arjuna said, "O Krishna, seeing my kinsmen arrayed here, eager to fight, kṛpayā parayā’’viṣṭo viṣīdannidamabravīt | dṛṣṭvemaṃ svajanaṃ kṛṣṇa yuyutsuṃ samupasthitam ||

nodes.d: My limbs fail, my mouth is parched, my body quivers, and my hair stands on end.
nodes.text: My limbs fail, my mouth is parched, my body quivers, and my hair stands on end. sīdanti mama gātrāṇi mukhaṃ ca pariśuṣyati | vepathuśca śarīre me romaharṣaśca jāyate ||

nodes.d: The Gandiva slips from my hand, and my skin burns all over; I am unable to stand, and my mind is reeling, as it were.
nodes.text: The Gandiva slips from my hand, and my skin burns all over; I am unable to stand, and my mind is reeling, as it were. gāṇḍīvaṃ sraṃsate hastāttvakcaiva paridahyate | na ca śaknomyavasthātuṃ bhramatīva ca me manaḥ ||

nodes.d: And I see ill omens, O Kesava. I do not see any good in slaying my kinsmen in battle.
nodes.text: And I see ill omens, O Kesava. I do not see any good in slaying my kinsmen in battle. nimittāni ca paśyāmi viparītāni keśava | na ca śreyo’nupaśyāmi hatvā svajanamāhave ||

nodes.d: I desire not victory, O Krishna, nor kingdom, nor pleasures. What use is dominion to us, O Krishna, or pleasures or even life?
nodes.text: I desire not victory, O Krishna, nor kingdom, nor pleasures. What use is dominion to us, O Krishna, or pleasures or even life? na kāṅkṣe vijayaṃ kṛṣṇa na ca rājyaṃ sukhāni ca | kiṃ no rājyena govinda kiṃ bhogairjīvitena vā ||

nodes.d: Those for whose sake we desire kingdom, enjoyments, and pleasures stand here in battle, having renounced life and wealth.
nodes.text: Those for whose sake we desire kingdom, enjoyments, and pleasures stand here in battle, having renounced life and wealth. yeṣāmarthe kāṅkṣitaṃ no rājyaṃ bhogāḥ sukhāni ca | ta ime’vasthitā yuddhe prāṇāṃstyaktvā dhanāni ca ||

nodes.d: Teachers, fathers, sons, and grandfathers, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other relatives—
nodes.text: Teachers, fathers, sons, and grandfathers, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other relatives— ācāryāḥ pitaraḥ putrāstathaiva ca pitāmahāḥ | mātulāḥ ścaśurāḥ pautrāḥ śyālāḥ sambandhinastathā ||

nodes.d: These I do not wish to kill, O Krishna, even though they kill me, for the sake of dominion over the three worlds; leave alone killing them for the sake of the earth."
nodes.text: These I do not wish to kill, O Krishna, even though they kill me, for the sake of dominion over the three worlds; leave alone killing them for the sake of the earth." etānna hantumicchāmi ghnato’pi madhusūdana | api trailokyarājyasya hetoḥ kiṃ nu mahīkṛte ||

nodes.d: By killing these sons of Dhritarashtra, what pleasure could be ours, O Janardana? Only sin would accrue to us from killing these felons.
nodes.text: By killing these sons of Dhritarashtra, what pleasure could be ours, O Janardana? Only sin would accrue to us from killing these felons. nihatya dhārtarāṣṭrānnaḥ kā prītiḥ syājjanārdana | pāpamevāśrayedasmānhatvaitānātatāyinaḥ ||

nodes.d: Therefore, we should not kill the sons of Dhritarashtra, our relatives; for how can we be happy by killing our own kin, O Madhava (Krishna)?
nodes.text: Therefore, we should not kill the sons of Dhritarashtra, our relatives; for how can we be happy by killing our own kin, O Madhava (Krishna)? tasmānnārhā vayaṃ hantuṃ dhārtarāṣṭrānsvabāndhavān | svajanaṃ hi kathaṃ hatvā sukhinaḥ syāma mādhava ||

nodes.d: Though they, with intelligence overpowered by greed, see no evil in the destruction of families and no sin in hostility to friends,
nodes.text: Though they, with intelligence overpowered by greed, see no evil in the destruction of families and no sin in hostility to friends, yadyapyete na paśyanti lobhopahatacetasaḥ | kulakṣayakṛtaṃ doṣaṃ mitradrohe ca pātakam ||

nodes.d: Why should we not, who clearly see the evil in the destruction of families, learn to turn away from this sin, O Janardana (Krishna)?
nodes.text: Why should we not, who clearly see the evil in the destruction of families, learn to turn away from this sin, O Janardana (Krishna)? kathaṃ na jñeyamasmābhiḥ pāpādasmānnivartitum | kulakṣayakṛtaṃ doṣaṃ prapaśyadbhirjanārdana ||

nodes.d: In the destruction of a family, the immemorial religious rites of that family perish; on the destruction of spirituality, impiety indeed, overwhelms the whole family.
nodes.text: In the destruction of a family, the immemorial religious rites of that family perish; on the destruction of spirituality, impiety indeed, overwhelms the whole family. kulakṣaye praṇaśyanti kuladharmāḥ sanātanāḥ | dharme naṣṭe kulaṃ kṛtsnamadharmo’bhibhavatyuta ||

nodes.d: O Krishna, by the prevalence of impiety, the women of the family become corrupt; and, when women are corrupted, O Varshenya (descendant of Vrishni), intermingling of castes arises.
nodes.text: O Krishna, by the prevalence of impiety, the women of the family become corrupt; and, when women are corrupted, O Varshenya (descendant of Vrishni), intermingling of castes arises. adharmābhibhavātkṛṣṇa praduṣyanti kulastriyaḥ | strīṣu duṣṭāsu vārṣṇeya jāyate varṇasaṅkaraḥ ||

nodes.d: Confusion of castes leads to hell for the slayers of the family, for their forebears fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and libations of water.
nodes.text: Confusion of castes leads to hell for the slayers of the family, for their forebears fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and libations of water. saṅkaro narakāyaiva kulaghnānāṃ kulasya ca | patanti pitaro hyeṣāṃ luptapiṇḍodakakriyāḥ ||

nodes.d: By these evil deeds of the destroyers of the family, which cause confusion of castes, the eternal religious rites of the caste and the family are destroyed.
nodes.text: By these evil deeds of the destroyers of the family, which cause confusion of castes, the eternal religious rites of the caste and the family are destroyed. doṣairetaiḥ kulaghnānāṃ varṇasaṅkarakārakaiḥ | utsādyante jātidharmāḥ kuladharmāśca śāśvatāḥ ||

nodes.d: We have heard, O Janardana, that those men in whose families the religious practices have been destroyed are inevitably destined to dwell in hell for an unknown period.
nodes.text: We have heard, O Janardana, that those men in whose families the religious practices have been destroyed are inevitably destined to dwell in hell for an unknown period. utsannakuladharmāṇāṃ manuṣyāṇāṃ janārdana | narake’niyataṃ vāso bhavatītyanuśuśruma ||

nodes.d: Alas! We are involved in a great sin, for we are prepared to kill our kinsmen, out of greed for the pleasures of a kingdom.
nodes.text: Alas! We are involved in a great sin, for we are prepared to kill our kinsmen, out of greed for the pleasures of a kingdom. aho bata mahatpāpaṃ kartuṃ vyavasitā vayam | yadrājyasukhalobhena hantuṃ svajanamudyatāḥ ||

nodes.d: If the sons of Dhritarashtra, with weapons in hand, should slay me in battle, unresisting and unarmed, that would be better for me.
nodes.text: If the sons of Dhritarashtra, with weapons in hand, should slay me in battle, unresisting and unarmed, that would be better for me. yadi māmapratīkāramaśastraṃ śastrapāṇayaḥ | dhārtarāṣṭrā raṇe hanyustanme kṣemataraṃ bhavet ||

nodes.d: Sanjaya said, Having thus spoken in the midst of the battlefield, Arjuna cast away his bow and arrow and, his mind overwhelmed with sorrow, sat down on the seat of the chariot.
nodes.text: Sanjaya said, Having thus spoken in the midst of the battlefield, Arjuna cast away his bow and arrow and, his mind overwhelmed with sorrow, sat down on the seat of the chariot. evamuktvā’rjunaḥ saṃkhye rathopastha upāviśat | visṛjya saśaraṃ cāpaṃ śokasaṃvignamānasaḥ ||

nodes.d: Sanjaya said: To him, who was thus overcome with pity, despondent, with eyes full of tears and agitated, Madhusudana (the destroyer of Madhu) or Krishna spoke these words.
nodes.text: Sanjaya said: To him, who was thus overcome with pity, despondent, with eyes full of tears and agitated, Madhusudana (the destroyer of Madhu) or Krishna spoke these words. taṃ tathā kṛpayā’viṣṭamaśrupūrṇākulekṣaṇam | viṣīdantamidaṃ vākyamuvāca madhusūdanaḥ ||

nodes.d: The Blessed Lord said, "From whence has this perilous strait come upon you, this dejection which is unworthy of you, disgraceful, and which will close the gates of heaven upon…
nodes.text: The Blessed Lord said, "From whence has this perilous strait come upon you, this dejection which is unworthy of you, disgraceful, and which will close the gates of heaven upon… kutastvā kaśmalamidaṃ viṣame samupasthitam | anāryajuṣṭamasvargyamakīrtikaramarjuna ||

nodes.d: Do not yield to impotence, O Arjuna, son of Pritha. It does not befit you. Cast off this mean weakness of the heart! Stand up, O conqueror of foes!
nodes.text: Do not yield to impotence, O Arjuna, son of Pritha. It does not befit you. Cast off this mean weakness of the heart! Stand up, O conqueror of foes! klaibyaṃ mā sma gamaḥ pārtha naitattvayyupapadyate | kṣudraṃ hṛdayadaurbalyaṃ tyaktvottiṣṭha parantapa ||

nodes.d: Arjuna said, "O Madhusudana, how can I fight in battle with arrows against Bhishma and Drona, who are worthy of being worshipped, O destroyer of enemies?"
nodes.text: Arjuna said, "O Madhusudana, how can I fight in battle with arrows against Bhishma and Drona, who are worthy of being worshipped, O destroyer of enemies?" kathaṃ bhīṣmamahaṃ saṃkhye droṇaṃ ca madhusūdana | iṣubhiḥ pratiyotsyāmi pūjārhāvarisūdana ||

nodes.d: Better it is, indeed, in this world to accept alms than to slay the most noble teachers. But if I were to kill them, even in this world, all my enjoyments of wealth and…
nodes.text: Better it is, indeed, in this world to accept alms than to slay the most noble teachers. But if I were to kill them, even in this world, all my enjoyments of wealth and… gurūnahatvā hi mahānubhāvān śreyo bhoktuṃ bhaikṣyamapīha loke | hatvārthakāmāṃstu gurūnihaiva bhuñjīya bhogān rudhirapradigdhān ||

nodes.d: I can hardly tell which would be better, that we should conquer them or that they should conquer us. Even the sons of Dhritarashtra, whom we do not wish to slay, stand facing us.
nodes.text: I can hardly tell which would be better, that we should conquer them or that they should conquer us. Even the sons of Dhritarashtra, whom we do not wish to slay, stand facing us. na caitadvidmaḥ kataranno garīyo yadvā jayema yadi vā no jayeyuḥ | yāneva hatvā na jijīviṣāma ste’vasthitāḥ pramukhe dhārtarāṣṭrāḥ ||

nodes.d: My heart is overpowered by the taint of pity; my mind is confused as to my duty. I ask Thee: Tell me decisively what is good for me. I am Thy disciple; instruct me, who has…
nodes.text: My heart is overpowered by the taint of pity; my mind is confused as to my duty. I ask Thee: Tell me decisively what is good for me. I am Thy disciple; instruct me, who has… kārpaṇyadoṣopahatasvabhāvaḥ pṛcchāmi tvāṃ dharmasaṃmūḍhacetāḥ | yacchreyaḥ syānniścitaṃ brūhi tanme śiṣyaste’haṃ śādhi māṃ tvāṃ prapannam ||

nodes.d: I do not see that this sorrow that burns up my senses would be removed, even if I were to attain prosperous and unrivaled dominion on earth or lordship over the gods.
nodes.text: I do not see that this sorrow that burns up my senses would be removed, even if I were to attain prosperous and unrivaled dominion on earth or lordship over the gods. na hi prapaśyāmi mamāpanudyā dyacchokamucchoṣaṇamindriyāṇām | avāpya bhūmāvasapatnamṛddham rājyaṃ surāṇāmapi cādhipatyam ||

nodes.d: Sanjaya said: Having spoken thus to Hrishikesha, the Lord of the senses, Arjuna, the conqueror of sleep and destroyer of foes, said, "I will not fight," and became silent.
nodes.text: Sanjaya said: Having spoken thus to Hrishikesha, the Lord of the senses, Arjuna, the conqueror of sleep and destroyer of foes, said, "I will not fight," and became silent. evamuktvā hṛṣīkeśaṃ guḍākeśaḥ parantapa | na yotsya iti govindamuktvā tūṣṇīṃ babhūva ha ||

nodes.d: To him who was despondent in the midst of the two armies, Krishna, smiling, O Bharata, spoke these words.
nodes.text: To him who was despondent in the midst of the two armies, Krishna, smiling, O Bharata, spoke these words. tamuvāca hṛṣīkeśaḥ prahasanniva bhārata | senayorubhayormadhye viṣīdantamidaṃ vacaḥ ||

nodes.d: The Blessed Lord said, "You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for; yet, you speak words of wisdom. The wise grieve neither for the living nor for the dead."
nodes.text: The Blessed Lord said, "You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for; yet, you speak words of wisdom. The wise grieve neither for the living nor for the dead." aśocyānanvaśocastvaṃ prajñāvādāṃśca bhāṣase | gatāsūnagatāsūṃśca nānuśocanti paṇḍitāḥ ||

nodes.d: Nor, at any time, was I not, nor thou, nor these rulers of men; nor, verily, shall we ever cease to be hereafter.
nodes.text: Nor, at any time, was I not, nor thou, nor these rulers of men; nor, verily, shall we ever cease to be hereafter. na tvevāhaṃ jātu nāsaṃ na tvaṃ neme janādhipāḥ | na caiva na bhaviṣyāmaḥ sarve vayamataḥ param ||

nodes.d: Just as the embodied soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so too does it pass into another body; the steadfast one does not grieve over this.
nodes.text: Just as the embodied soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so too does it pass into another body; the steadfast one does not grieve over this. dehino’sminyathā dehe kaumāraṃ yauvanaṃ jarā | tathā dehāntaraprāptirdhīrastatra na muhyati ||

nodes.d: The contact of the senses with the objects, O son of Kunti, which causes heat and cold, pleasure and pain, has a beginning and an end; they are impermanent; endure them…
nodes.text: The contact of the senses with the objects, O son of Kunti, which causes heat and cold, pleasure and pain, has a beginning and an end; they are impermanent; endure them… mātrāsparśāstu kaunteya śītoṣṇasukhaduḥkhadāḥ | āgamāpāyino’nityāstāṃstitikṣasva bhārata ||

nodes.d: That firm man, whom surely these afflictions do not, O chief among men, to whom pleasure and pain are the same, is fit for attaining immortality.
nodes.text: That firm man, whom surely these afflictions do not, O chief among men, to whom pleasure and pain are the same, is fit for attaining immortality. yaṃ hi na vyathayantyete puruṣaṃ puruṣarṣabha | samaduḥkhasukhaṃ dhīraṃ so’mṛtatvāya kalpate ||

nodes.d: The unreal has no being; there is no non-being of the real; the truth about both has been seen by the knowers of the truth (or the seers of the essence).
nodes.text: The unreal has no being; there is no non-being of the real; the truth about both has been seen by the knowers of the truth (or the seers of the essence). nāsato vidyate bhāvo nābhāvo vidyate sataḥ | ubhayorapi dṛṣṭo’ntastvanayostattvadarśibhiḥ ||

nodes.d: Know that to be indestructible, by which all this is pervaded. No one can cause the destruction of that, the Imperishable.
nodes.text: Know that to be indestructible, by which all this is pervaded. No one can cause the destruction of that, the Imperishable. avināśi tu tadviddhi yena sarvamidaṃ tatam | vināśamavyayasyāsya na kaścit kartumarhati ||

nodes.d: These bodies of the embodied Self, which are eternal, indestructible, and immeasurable, are said to have an end. Therefore, fight, O Arjuna.
nodes.text: These bodies of the embodied Self, which are eternal, indestructible, and immeasurable, are said to have an end. Therefore, fight, O Arjuna. antavanta ime dehā nityasyoktāḥ śarīriṇaḥ | anāśino’prameyasya tasmādyudhyasva bhārata ||

nodes.d: He who takes the Self to be the slayer and he who thinks it is slain, neither of them knows. It does not slay, nor is it slain.
nodes.text: He who takes the Self to be the slayer and he who thinks it is slain, neither of them knows. It does not slay, nor is it slain. ya enaṃ vetti hantāraṃ yaścainaṃ manyate hatam | ubhau tau na vijānīto nāyaṃ hanti na hanyate ||

nodes.d: It is not born, nor does it ever die; after having been, it again does not cease to be; unborn, eternal, changeless, and ancient, it is not killed when the body is killed.
nodes.text: It is not born, nor does it ever die; after having been, it again does not cease to be; unborn, eternal, changeless, and ancient, it is not killed when the body is killed. na jāyate mriyate vā kadāci nnāyaṃ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ | ajo nityaḥ śāśvato’yaṃ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre ||

nodes.d: Whoever knows it to be indestructible, eternal, unborn, and inexhaustible, how can that person slay, O Arjuna, or cause to be slain?
nodes.text: Whoever knows it to be indestructible, eternal, unborn, and inexhaustible, how can that person slay, O Arjuna, or cause to be slain? vedāvināśinaṃ nityaṃ ya enamajamavyayam | kathaṃ sa puruṣaḥ pārtha kaṃ ghātayati hanti kam ||

nodes.d: Just as a man casts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so too the embodied Self casts off worn-out bodies and enters others that are new.
nodes.text: Just as a man casts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so too the embodied Self casts off worn-out bodies and enters others that are new. vāsāṃsi jīrṇāni yathā vihāya navāni gṛhṇāti naro’parāṇi | tathā śarīrāṇi vihāya jīrṇā nyanyāni saṃyāti navāni dehī ||

nodes.d: Weapons cannot cut it, fire cannot burn it, water cannot wet it, wind cannot dry it.
nodes.text: Weapons cannot cut it, fire cannot burn it, water cannot wet it, wind cannot dry it. nainaṃ chindanti śastrāṇi nainaṃ dahati pāvakaḥ | na cainaṃ kledayantyāpo na śoṣayati mārutaḥ ||

nodes.d: This Self cannot be cut, burned, wetted, nor dried up; it is eternal, all-pervasive, stable, immovable, and ancient.
nodes.text: This Self cannot be cut, burned, wetted, nor dried up; it is eternal, all-pervasive, stable, immovable, and ancient. acchedyo’yamadāhyo’yamakledyo’śoṣya eva ca | nityaḥ sarvagataḥ sthāṇuracalo’yaṃ sanātanaḥ ||

nodes.d: This Self is said to be unmanifested, unthinkable, and unchangeable. Therefore, knowing this to be so, you should not grieve.
nodes.text: This Self is said to be unmanifested, unthinkable, and unchangeable. Therefore, knowing this to be so, you should not grieve. avyakto’yamacintyo’yamavikāryo’yamucyate | tasmādevaṃ viditvainaṃ nānuśocitumarhasi ||

nodes.d: But even if thou thinkest of It as constantly being born and constantly dying, even then, O mighty-armed one, thou shouldst not grieve.
nodes.text: But even if thou thinkest of It as constantly being born and constantly dying, even then, O mighty-armed one, thou shouldst not grieve. atha cainaṃ nityajātaṃ nityaṃ vā manyase mṛtam | tathāpi tvaṃ mahābāho naivaṃ śocitumarhasi ||

nodes.d: For the born, death is certain, and for the dead, birth is certain; therefore, you should not grieve over the inevitable.
nodes.text: For the born, death is certain, and for the dead, birth is certain; therefore, you should not grieve over the inevitable. jātasya hi dhruvo mṛtyurdhruvaṃ janma mṛtasya ca | tasmādaparihārye’rthe na tvaṃ śocitumarhasi ||

nodes.d: Beings are unmanifest in their beginning, manifest in their middle state, O Arjuna, and unmanifest again in their end. What is there to grieve about?
nodes.text: Beings are unmanifest in their beginning, manifest in their middle state, O Arjuna, and unmanifest again in their end. What is there to grieve about? avyaktādīni bhūtāni vyaktamadhyāni bhārata | avyaktanidhanānyeva tatra kā paridevanā ||

nodes.d: One sees this (the Self) as a wonder; another speaks of it as a wonder; another hears of it as a wonder; yet, having heard, none understands it at all.
nodes.text: One sees this (the Self) as a wonder; another speaks of it as a wonder; another hears of it as a wonder; yet, having heard, none understands it at all. āścaryavatpaśyati kaścidena māścaryavadvadati tathaiva cānyaḥ | āścaryavaccainamanyaḥ śrṛṇoti śrutvāpyenaṃ veda na caiva kaścit ||

nodes.d: This indweller in the body of everyone is ever indestructible, O Arjuna; therefore, you should not grieve for any creature.
nodes.text: This indweller in the body of everyone is ever indestructible, O Arjuna; therefore, you should not grieve for any creature. dehī nityamavadhyo’yaṃ dehe sarvasya bhārata | tasmātsarvāṇi bhūtāni na tvaṃ śocitumarhasi ||

nodes.d: Further, having regard to your duty, you should not waver, for there is nothing higher for a Kshatriya than a righteous war.
nodes.text: Further, having regard to your duty, you should not waver, for there is nothing higher for a Kshatriya than a righteous war. svadharmamapi cāvekṣya na vikampitumarhasi | dharmyāddhi yuddhāchreyo’nyatkṣatriyasya na vidyate ||

nodes.d: Happy are the Kshatriyas, O Arjuna! who are called to fight in such a battle that comes of its own accord as an open door to heaven.
nodes.text: Happy are the Kshatriyas, O Arjuna! who are called to fight in such a battle that comes of its own accord as an open door to heaven. yadṛcchayā copapannaṃ svargadvāramapāvṛtam | sukhinaḥ kṣatriyāḥ pārtha labhante yuddhamīdṛśam ||

nodes.d: But if you will not fight this righteous war, then having abandoned your own duty and reputation, you will incur sin.
nodes.text: But if you will not fight this righteous war, then having abandoned your own duty and reputation, you will incur sin. atha caittvamimaṃ dharmyaṃ saṃgrāmaṃ na kariṣyasi | tataḥ svadharmaṃ kīrtiṃ ca hitvā pāpamavāpsyasi ||

nodes.d: People will also recount your everlasting dishonor; and for one who has been honored, dishonor is worse than death.
nodes.text: People will also recount your everlasting dishonor; and for one who has been honored, dishonor is worse than death. akīrtiṃ cāpi bhūtāni kathayiṣyanti te’vyayām | saṃbhāvitasya cākīrtirmaraṇādatiricyate ||

nodes.d: The great chariot-warriors will think that you have withdrawn from the battle out of fear, and you will be held in low esteem by those who have held you in high regard.
nodes.text: The great chariot-warriors will think that you have withdrawn from the battle out of fear, and you will be held in low esteem by those who have held you in high regard. bhayādraṇāduparataṃ maṃsyante tvāṃ mahārathāḥ | yeṣāṃ ca tvaṃ bahumato bhūtvā yāsyasi lāghavam ||

nodes.d: Your enemies, scoffing at your power, will speak many abusive words—what could be more painful than this?
nodes.text: Your enemies, scoffing at your power, will speak many abusive words—what could be more painful than this? avācyavādāṃśca bahūn vadiṣyanti tavāhitāḥ | nindantastava sāmarthyaṃ tato duḥkhataraṃ nu kim ||

nodes.d: Slain, you will obtain heaven; victorious, you will enjoy the earth; therefore, stand up, O son of Kunti, resolved to fight.
nodes.text: Slain, you will obtain heaven; victorious, you will enjoy the earth; therefore, stand up, O son of Kunti, resolved to fight. hato vā prāpsyasi svargaṃ jitvā vā bhokṣyase mahīm | tasmāduttiṣṭha kaunteya yuddhāya kṛtaniścayaḥ ||

nodes.d: Having made pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat equal, engage in battle for the sake of battle; thus, you shall not incur sin.
nodes.text: Having made pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat equal, engage in battle for the sake of battle; thus, you shall not incur sin. sukhaduḥkhe same kṛtvā lābhālābhau jayājayau | tato yuddhāya yujyasva naivaṃ pāpamavāpsyasi ||

nodes.d: This, which has been taught to you, is wisdom concerning Sankhya. Now listen to wisdom concerning Yoga, endowed with which, O Arjuna, you shall cast off the bonds of action.
nodes.text: This, which has been taught to you, is wisdom concerning Sankhya. Now listen to wisdom concerning Yoga, endowed with which, O Arjuna, you shall cast off the bonds of action. eṣā te’bhihitā sāṃkhye buddhiryoge tvimāṃ śrṛṇu | buddhyāyukto yayā pārtha karmabandhaṃ prahāsyasi ||

nodes.d: In this, there is no loss of effort, nor is there any harm produced, nor any transgression. Even a little of this knowledge protects one from great fear.
nodes.text: In this, there is no loss of effort, nor is there any harm produced, nor any transgression. Even a little of this knowledge protects one from great fear. nehābhikramanāśo’sti pratyavāyo na vidyate | svalpamapyasya dharmasya trāyate mahato bhayāt ||

nodes.d: Here, O joy of the Kurus, there is only one single-pointed determination; many-branched and endless are the thoughts of the indecisive.
nodes.text: Here, O joy of the Kurus, there is only one single-pointed determination; many-branched and endless are the thoughts of the indecisive. vyavasāyātmikā buddhirekeha kurunandana | bahuśākhā hyanantāśca buddhayo’vyavasāyinām ||

nodes.d: The unwise, taking pleasure in the eulogizing words of the Vedas, utter flowery speech, saying, "There is nothing else," O Arjuna.
nodes.text: The unwise, taking pleasure in the eulogizing words of the Vedas, utter flowery speech, saying, "There is nothing else," O Arjuna. yāmimāṃ puṣpitāṃ vācaṃ pravadantyavipaścitaḥ | vedavādaratāḥ pārtha nānyadastīti vādinaḥ ||

nodes.d: Full of desires, with heaven as their goal, (they speak words that are directed to ends) leading to new births as the result of their works, and prescribe various methods…
nodes.text: Full of desires, with heaven as their goal, (they speak words that are directed to ends) leading to new births as the result of their works, and prescribe various methods… kāmātmānaḥ svargaparā janmakarmaphalapradām | kriyāviśeṣabahulāṃ bhogaiśvaryagatiṃ prati ||

nodes.d: For those who are attached to pleasure and power, whose minds are drawn away by such teachings, their determinate reason is not formed which is steadily bent on meditation and…
nodes.text: For those who are attached to pleasure and power, whose minds are drawn away by such teachings, their determinate reason is not formed which is steadily bent on meditation and… bhogaiśvaryaprasaktānāṃ tayāpahṛtacetasām | vyavasāyātmikā buddhiḥ samādhau na vidhīyate ||

nodes.d: The Vedas deal with the three attributes; be thou above these three attributes. O Arjuna, free yourself from the pairs of opposites and ever remain in the quality of Sattva,…
nodes.text: The Vedas deal with the three attributes; be thou above these three attributes. O Arjuna, free yourself from the pairs of opposites and ever remain in the quality of Sattva,… traiguṇyaviṣayā vedā nistraiguṇyo bhavārjuna | nirdvandvo nityasattvastho niryogakṣema ātmavān ||

nodes.d: To the Brahmana who has known the Self, all the Vedas are of as much use as a reservoir of water would be in a place where there is a flood.
nodes.text: To the Brahmana who has known the Self, all the Vedas are of as much use as a reservoir of water would be in a place where there is a flood. yāvānartha udapāne sarvataḥ saṃplutodake | tāvānsarveṣu vedeṣu brāhmaṇasya vijānataḥ ||

nodes.d: Your right is only to work, but not to its results; do not let the results of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction.
nodes.text: Your right is only to work, but not to its results; do not let the results of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction. karmaṇyevādhikāraste mā phaleṣu kadācana | mā karmaphalaheturbhūrmā te saṅgo’stvakarmaṇi ||

nodes.d: Perform action, O Arjuna, being steadfast in Yoga, abandoning attachment and balanced in success and failure; evenness of mind is called Yoga.
nodes.text: Perform action, O Arjuna, being steadfast in Yoga, abandoning attachment and balanced in success and failure; evenness of mind is called Yoga. yogasthaḥ kuru karmāṇi saṅgaṃ tyaktvā dhanañjaya | siddhyasiddhyoḥ samo bhūtvā samatvaṃ yoga ucyate ||

nodes.d: Far lower than the Yoga of wisdom is action, O Arjuna. Seek thou refuge in wisdom; wretched are those whose motive is the fruit.
nodes.text: Far lower than the Yoga of wisdom is action, O Arjuna. Seek thou refuge in wisdom; wretched are those whose motive is the fruit. dūreṇa hyavaraṃ karma buddhiyogāddhanañjaya | buddhau śaraṇamanviccha kṛpaṇāḥ phalahetavaḥ ||

nodes.d: Endowed with wisdom and evenness of mind, one casts off in this life both good and evil deeds; therefore, devote yourself to Yoga; Yoga is skill in action.
nodes.text: Endowed with wisdom and evenness of mind, one casts off in this life both good and evil deeds; therefore, devote yourself to Yoga; Yoga is skill in action. buddhiyukto jahātīha ubhe sukṛtaduṣkṛte | tasmādyogāya yujyasva yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam ||

nodes.d: The wise, possessing knowledge, having abandoned the fruits of their actions, and being freed from the bonds of birth, go to the place which is beyond all evil.
nodes.text: The wise, possessing knowledge, having abandoned the fruits of their actions, and being freed from the bonds of birth, go to the place which is beyond all evil. karmajaṃ buddhiyuktā hi phalaṃ tyaktvā manīṣiṇaḥ | janmabandhavinirmuktāḥ padaṃ gacchantyanāmayam ||

nodes.d: When your intellect passes beyond the mire of delusion, then you will attain indifference to what has been heard and what has yet to be heard.
nodes.text: When your intellect passes beyond the mire of delusion, then you will attain indifference to what has been heard and what has yet to be heard. yadā te mohakalilaṃ buddhirvyatitariṣyati | tadā gantāsi nirvedaṃ śrotavyasya śrutasya ca ||

nodes.d: When your intellect, which is perplexed by the Vedic texts you have read, stands immovable and steady in the Self, then you will attain Self-realization.
nodes.text: When your intellect, which is perplexed by the Vedic texts you have read, stands immovable and steady in the Self, then you will attain Self-realization. śrutivipratipannā te yadā sthāsyati niścalā | samādhāvacalā buddhistadā yogamavāpsyasi ||

nodes.d: Arjuna said, "O Krishna, what is the description of one who has steady wisdom and is merged in the superconscious state? How does one of steady wisdom speak, how do they sit,…
nodes.text: Arjuna said, "O Krishna, what is the description of one who has steady wisdom and is merged in the superconscious state? How does one of steady wisdom speak, how do they sit,… sthitaprajñasya kā bhāṣā samādhisthasya keśava | sthitadhīḥ kiṃ prabhāṣeta kimāsīta vrajeta kim ||

nodes.d: The Blessed Lord said, "When a man completely casts off, O Arjuna, all the desires of the mind and is satisfied in the Self by the Self, then he is said to be one of steady…
nodes.text: The Blessed Lord said, "When a man completely casts off, O Arjuna, all the desires of the mind and is satisfied in the Self by the Self, then he is said to be one of steady… prajahāti yadā kāmān sarvān pārtha manogatān | ātmanyevātmanā tuṣṭaḥ sthitaprajñastadocyate ||

nodes.d: He whose mind is not shaken by adversity, who does not long for pleasures, and is free from attachment, fear, and anger, is called a sage of steady wisdom.
nodes.text: He whose mind is not shaken by adversity, who does not long for pleasures, and is free from attachment, fear, and anger, is called a sage of steady wisdom. duḥkheṣvanudvignamanāḥ sukheṣu vigataspṛhaḥ | vītarāgabhayakrodhaḥ sthitadhīrmunirucyate ||

nodes.d: He who is everywhere without attachment, upon encountering anything good or bad, neither rejoices nor hastens; his wisdom is firm.
nodes.text: He who is everywhere without attachment, upon encountering anything good or bad, neither rejoices nor hastens; his wisdom is firm. yaḥ sarvatrānabhisnehastattatprāpya śubhāśubham | nābhinandati na dveṣṭi tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā ||

nodes.d: When, like the tortoise which withdraws all its limbs on all sides, he withdraws his senses from the sense-objects, then his wisdom becomes steady.
nodes.text: When, like the tortoise which withdraws all its limbs on all sides, he withdraws his senses from the sense-objects, then his wisdom becomes steady. yadā saṃharate cāyaṃ kūrmo’ṅgānīva sarvaśaḥ | indriyāṇīndriyārthebhyastasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā ||

nodes.d: The objects of the senses turn away from the abstinent man, leaving the longing behind; but his longing also turns away upon seeing the Supreme.
nodes.text: The objects of the senses turn away from the abstinent man, leaving the longing behind; but his longing also turns away upon seeing the Supreme. viṣayā vinivartante nirāhārasya dehinaḥ | rasavarjaṃ raso’pyasya paraṃ dṛṣṭvā nivartate ||

nodes.d: The turbulent senses, O Arjuna, can violently carry away the mind of a wise person, even though they are striving to control them.
nodes.text: The turbulent senses, O Arjuna, can violently carry away the mind of a wise person, even though they are striving to control them. yatato hyapi kaunteya puruṣasya vipaścitaḥ | indriyāṇi pramāthīni haranti prasabhaṃ manaḥ ||

nodes.d: Having restrained them all, he should sit steadfast, intent on Me; his wisdom is steady whose senses are under control.
nodes.text: Having restrained them all, he should sit steadfast, intent on Me; his wisdom is steady whose senses are under control. tāni sarvāṇi saṃyamya yukta āsīta matparaḥ | vaśe hi yasyendriyāṇi tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā ||

nodes.d: When one thinks of objects, attachment to them arises; from attachment, desire is born; from desire, anger arises.
nodes.text: When one thinks of objects, attachment to them arises; from attachment, desire is born; from desire, anger arises. dhyāyato viṣayānpuṃsaḥ saṅgasteṣūpajāyate | saṅgāt saṃjāyate kāmaḥ kāmātkrodho’bhijāyate ||

nodes.d: Anger leads to delusion, which causes loss of memory; this, in turn, leads to the destruction of discrimination, resulting in destruction.
nodes.text: Anger leads to delusion, which causes loss of memory; this, in turn, leads to the destruction of discrimination, resulting in destruction. krodhādbhavati saṃmohaḥ saṃmohātsmṛtivibhramaḥ | smṛtibhraṃśād buddhināśo buddhināśātpraṇaśyati ||

nodes.d: But the self-controlled man, moving among objects with the senses restrained and free from attraction and repulsion, attains peace.
nodes.text: But the self-controlled man, moving among objects with the senses restrained and free from attraction and repulsion, attains peace. rāgadveṣaviyuktaistu viṣayānindriyaiścaran | ātmavaśyairvidheyātmā prasādamadhigacchati ||

nodes.d: In that peace, all pains are destroyed; for the intellect of the tranquil-minded soon becomes steady.
nodes.text: In that peace, all pains are destroyed; for the intellect of the tranquil-minded soon becomes steady. prasāde sarvaduḥkhānāṃ hānirasyopajāyate | prasannacetaso hyāśu buddhiḥ paryavatiṣṭhate ||

nodes.d: There is no knowledge of the Self for the unsteady, and no meditation is possible for the unsteady, and no peace for the unmeditative, and how can there be happiness for one…
nodes.text: There is no knowledge of the Self for the unsteady, and no meditation is possible for the unsteady, and no peace for the unmeditative, and how can there be happiness for one… nāsti buddhirayuktasya na cāyuktasya bhāvanā | na cābhāvayataḥ śāntiraśāntasya kutaḥ sukham ||

nodes.d: For the mind, which follows in the wake of the wandering senses, carries away his discrimination, as the wind carries away a boat on the waters.
nodes.text: For the mind, which follows in the wake of the wandering senses, carries away his discrimination, as the wind carries away a boat on the waters. indriyāṇāṃ hi caratāṃ yanmano’nuvidhīyate | tadasya harati prajñāṃ vāyurnāvamivāmbhasi ||

nodes.d: Therefore, O mighty-armed Arjuna, his knowledge is steady whose senses are completely restrained from sense objects.
nodes.text: Therefore, O mighty-armed Arjuna, his knowledge is steady whose senses are completely restrained from sense objects. tasmādyasya mahābāho nigṛhītāni sarvaśaḥ | indriyāṇīndriyārthebhyastasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā ||

nodes.d: That which is night to all beings, in that the self-controlled man is awake; when all beings are awake, that is night for the sage who sees.
nodes.text: That which is night to all beings, in that the self-controlled man is awake; when all beings are awake, that is night for the sage who sees. yā niśā sarvabhūtānāṃ tasyāṃ jāgarti saṃyamī | yasyāṃ jāgrati bhūtāni sā niśā paśyato muneḥ ||

nodes.d: He attains peace into whom all desires enter, just as waters enter the ocean which, filled from all sides, remains unmoved; but not the man who is full of desires.
nodes.text: He attains peace into whom all desires enter, just as waters enter the ocean which, filled from all sides, remains unmoved; but not the man who is full of desires. āpūryamāṇamacalapratiṣṭhaṃ samudramāpaḥ praviśanti yadvat | tadvatkāmā yaṃ praviśanti sarve sa śāntimāpnoti na kāmakāmī ||

nodes.d: That person attains peace who, abandoning all desires, moves about without longing, without the sense of ownership, and without egoism.
nodes.text: That person attains peace who, abandoning all desires, moves about without longing, without the sense of ownership, and without egoism. vihāya kāmānyaḥ sarvānpumāṃścarati niḥspṛhaḥ | nirmamo nirahaṃkāraḥ sa śāṃtimadhigacchati ||

nodes.d: O son of Pritha, this is the eternal state, the Brahmic seat. Attaining this, one is not deluded. Being established in it, one attains oneness with Brahman even at the end of life.
nodes.text: O son of Pritha, this is the eternal state, the Brahmic seat. Attaining this, one is not deluded. Being established in it, one attains oneness with Brahman even at the end of life. eṣā brāhmī sthitiḥ pārtha naināṃ prāpya vimuhyati | sthitvā’syāmantakāle’pi brahmanirvāṇamṛcchati ||

nodes.d: Arjuna said: If Thou thinkest that knowledge is superior to action, O Krishna, why then, O Kesava, doest Thou ask me to engage in this terrible action?
nodes.text: Arjuna said: If Thou thinkest that knowledge is superior to action, O Krishna, why then, O Kesava, doest Thou ask me to engage in this terrible action? jyāyasī cetkarmaṇaste matā buddhirjanārdana | tatkiṃ karmaṇi ghore māṃ niyojayasi keśava ||

nodes.d: With this seemingly perplexing speech, you seem to be confusing my understanding; therefore, tell me one certain way by which I may attain bliss.
nodes.text: With this seemingly perplexing speech, you seem to be confusing my understanding; therefore, tell me one certain way by which I may attain bliss. vyāmiśreṇeva vākyena buddhiṃ mohayasīva me | tadekaṃ vada niścitya yena śreyo’hamāpnuyām ||

nodes.d: The Blessed Lord said, "In this world, there is a twofold path, as I said before, O sinless one: the path of knowledge of the Sankhyas and the path of action of the Yogins."
nodes.text: The Blessed Lord said, "In this world, there is a twofold path, as I said before, O sinless one: the path of knowledge of the Sankhyas and the path of action of the Yogins." loke’smindvividhā niṣṭhā purā proktā mayānagha | jñānayogena sāṃkhyānāṃ karmayogena yoginām ||

nodes.d: Man does not reach actionlessness by not performing actions; nor does he attain perfection by mere renunciation.
nodes.text: Man does not reach actionlessness by not performing actions; nor does he attain perfection by mere renunciation. na karmaṇāmanārambhānnaiṣkarmyaṃ puruṣo’śnute | na ca saṃnyasanādeva siddhiṃ samadhigacchati ||

nodes.d: Verily, no one can remain for even a moment without performing action; for everyone is made to act helplessly, indeed, by the qualities born of Nature.
nodes.text: Verily, no one can remain for even a moment without performing action; for everyone is made to act helplessly, indeed, by the qualities born of Nature. na hi kaścitkṣaṇamapi jātu tiṣṭhatyakarmakṛt | kāryate hyavaśaḥ karma sarvaḥ prakṛtijairguṇaiḥ ||

nodes.d: He who, restraining the organs of action, sits thinking of the sense-objects in his mind, he of deluded understanding is called a hypocrite.
nodes.text: He who, restraining the organs of action, sits thinking of the sense-objects in his mind, he of deluded understanding is called a hypocrite. karmendriyāṇi saṃyamya ya āste manasā smaran | indriyārthānvimūḍhātmā mithyācāraḥ sa ucyate ||

nodes.d: But whoever, controlling the senses by the mind, O Arjuna, engages himself in Karma Yoga with the organs of action, without attachment, he excels.
nodes.text: But whoever, controlling the senses by the mind, O Arjuna, engages himself in Karma Yoga with the organs of action, without attachment, he excels. yastvindriyāṇi manasā niyamyārabhate’rjuna | karmendriyaiḥ karmayogamasaktaḥ sa viśiṣyate ||

nodes.d: Perform your bounden duty, for action is superior to inaction, and even the maintenance of the body would not be possible for you through inaction.
